classification.difficultyReason: Explain why adding individual surface areas counts internal contact faces, identifying two hidden faces at each of the two joins.

inlines.text: Ed stacks three identical rectangular prisms on top of each other as shown.
He says “The surface area of my shape will be three times as large as the surface area of one of the rectangular prisms.”

spec.description: Unshaded shallow rectangular prism with a visible top and two side faces. Outside dimension arrows label both base directions and the height.
spec.mathematics: A rectangular prism with base dimensions 12 cm and 9 cm and height 2.5 cm. Explicit visible faces are A-B-Bt-At, D-A-At-Dt and At-Bt-Ct-Dt; rear bottom edges are occluded.
spec.answerVisibility: All dimensions are permanent student-visible givens.

spec.description: Three identical unshaded prisms with aligned footprints. Two joins extend across both visible side faces. The top face is visible; no dimensions are repeated.
spec.mathematics: Three layers of equal height and identical 12 cm by 9 cm footprints. Explicit visible faces are the two front side faces and top face; the two horizontal interfaces are internal.
spec.answerVisibility: Permanent student-visible comparison figure; no answer annotations.

answer.short: At each of the two joins, two faces become internal. Four faces are therefore no longer exposed, so the stack’s surface area is less than three times that of one prism.
answer.worked: Three times the surface area of one prism counts every face of all three prisms. At each join, the top face of the lower prism and the bottom face of the upper prism are hidden. There are two joins, so four faces must be excluded.
